claim: Deficient motivation contributes to numerous psychiatric disorders, including withdrawal from drug use, depression, schizophrenia, and others.
source: Deficient motivation contributes to numerous psychiatric disorders, including withdrawal from drug use, depression, schizophrenia, and others.
evidence: This is a general statement about psychiatric disorders that draws from established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: Nucleus accumbens (NAc) has been implicated in motivated behavior.
source: Nucleus accumbens (NAc) has been implicated in motivated behavior, but it remains unclear whether motivational drive is linked to discrete neurobiological mechanisms within the NAc.
evidence: This statement references established scientific knowledge about the NAc's role in motivation.

claim: Substantial variability in willingness to exert effort for reward was not associated with operant responding under low-effort conditions or stress levels.
source: We found that substantial variability in willingness to exert effort for reward was not associated with operant responding under low-effort conditions or stress levels.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from behavioral tests and corticosterone measurements presented in the manuscript.

claim: Effort-based motivation was mirrored by a divergent NAc shell transcriptome with differential regulation at potassium and dopamine signaling genes.
source: Instead, effort-based motivation was mirrored by a divergent NAc shell transcriptome with differential regulation at potassium and dopamine signaling genes.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA sequencing data presented in Figure 3.

claim: Motivation was inversely related to excitability of NAc principal neurons.
source: Functionally, motivation was inversely related to excitability of NAc principal neurons.
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological recordings showing increased firing in lowS animals presented in Figure 4.

claim: Neuronal and behavioral outputs associated with low motivation were linked to faster inactivation of a voltage-gated potassium channel, Kv1.4.
source: Furthermore, neuronal and behavioral outputs associated with low motivation were linked to faster inactivation of a voltage-gated potassium channel, Kv1.4.
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data showing faster IA decay times in lowS animals presented in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: Response to positive motivational situations has been proposed as one of only five behavioral dimensions that link the entire range of psychiatric diagnoses with underlying neurobiological mechanisms (RDoC framework; Cuthbert, 2015).
source: Indeed, response to positive motivational situations has been proposed as one of only five behavioral dimensions that link the entire range of psychiatric diagnoses with underlying neurobiological mechanisms (RDoC framework; Cuthbert, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Cuthbert, 2015.

claim: Chronically and persistently low motivation is associated with vulnerability to mental illness, including substance use disorders (Carroll et al., 2002; Janowsky et al., 2003; Perry et al., 2007; Radke et al., 2015; Brennan et al., 2001).
source: However, chronically and persistently low motivation is associated with vulnerability to mental illness, including substance use disorders (Carroll et al., 2002; Janowsky et al., 2003; Perry et al., 2007; Radke et al., 2015; Brennan et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: The nucleus accumbens integrates affective, spatial, and cognitive signals with approach to reward (Mogenson et al., 1980; Di Chiara, 2002; Di Chiara et al., 2004; Wise, 2004; Saddoris et al., 2015).
source: At the center of this circuit is the nucleus accumbens which integrates affective, spatial, and cognitive signals with approach to reward (Mogenson et al., 1980; Di Chiara, 2002; Di Chiara et al., 2004; Wise, 2004; Saddoris et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: The principal cells of the nucleus accumbens, striatal projection neurons (SPNs), regulate their firing patterns in a manner that predicts locomotion toward rewards as well as reward omission (Peoples and West, 1996; Nicola et al., 2004a; Roitman et al., 2005; Wan and Peoples, 2006).
source: The principal cells of the nucleus accumbens, striatal projection neurons (SPNs), regulate their firing patterns in a manner that predicts locomotion toward rewards as well as reward omission (Peoples and West, 1996; Nicola et al., 2004a; Roitman et al., 2005; Wan and Peoples, 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Action potential output of SPNs is modulated by dopamine, a molecule consistently implicated in behavioral response to motivationally salient stimuli, including action-outcome associations as well as reward avoidance (Akaike et al., 1987; Nicola et al., 2000; Ji and Martin, 2012; Ortinski et al., 2015).
source: Action potential output of SPNs is modulated by dopamine, a molecule consistently implicated in behavioral response to motivationally salient stimuli, including action-outcome associations as well as reward avoidance (Akaike et al., 1987; Nicola et al., 2000; Ji and Martin, 2012; Ortinski et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Dopamine modulates firing of SPNs in the nucleus accumbens via intracellular messengers coupled to the associated G-protein signaling cascades (Yang et al., 2013; Perez et al., 2006; Valdés-Baizabal et al., 2015; Cantrell et al., 1999; Schiffmann et al., 1995; Bender et al., 2010).
source: Dopamine modulates firing of SPNs in the nucleus accumbens via intracellular messengers coupled to the associated G-protein signaling cascades (Yang et al., 2013; Perez et al., 2006; Valdés-Baizabal et al., 2015; Cantrell et al., 1999; Schiffmann et al., 1995; Bender et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Voltage-gated potassium channels comprise the most diverse family of ion channels with over a hundred genes coding for potassium channel subunits in addition to multiple channel regulators.
source: Voltage-gated potassium channels comprise the most diverse family of ion channels with over a hundred genes coding for potassium channel subunits in addition to multiple channel regulators.
evidence: This statement draws from established scientific knowledge about potassium channels.

claim: Voltage-gated potassium channels are notably capable of suppressing, facilitating, and shaping action potentials and rhythmic activity throughout the central nervous system (Perez et al., 2006; Ji and Martin, 2014; Jan and Jan, 1997; Kimm et al., 2015; Johnston et al., 2010).
source: These channels are notably capable of suppressing, facilitating, and shaping action potentials and rhythmic activity throughout the central nervous system (Perez et al., 2006; Ji and Martin, 2014; Jan and Jan, 1997; Kimm et al., 2015; Johnston et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: In principal neurons of the medial nucleus of the trapezoid body, activation of Kv1 channels increases firing threshold and inhibits firing, while activation of Kv3 channels accelerates action potential repolarization and promotes high firing rates (Johnston et al., 2010).

claim: In midbrain dopaminergic neurons, inhibition of Kv2 channels increases action potential firing and decreases afterhyperpolarization (AHP), while activation of the large conductance Ca2+-activated K+ (BK) channel decreases AHP, but has no effect on action potential firing (Kimm et al., 2015).

source: In the striatum, dopamine depletion increases SPN intrinsic excitability and decreases AHP by accelerating the inactivation of the A-type (IA) K+ current (Azdad et al., 2009).

claim: Microinjection of a Kv7 agonist into the nucleus accumbens core has been found to reduce alcohol seeking (McGuier et al., 2016).

claim: Rats that compulsively self-administer methamphetamine despite negative consequences (foot shocks) are segregated from non-compulsive methamphetamine takers by both differential RNA expression and DNA hydroxymethylation at a number of genes encoding voltage-gated K+ channels (Cadet et al., 2017).
source: Finally, a genome-wide analysis found rats that compulsively self-administer methamphetamine despite negative consequences (foot shocks) are segregated from non-compulsive methamphetamine takers by both differential RNA expression and DNA hydroxymethylation at a number of genes encoding voltage-gated K+ channels (Cadet et al., 2017).

claim: HighS rats reached a mean breakpoint of 270.4 ± 11.3 lever presses, whereas lowS rats reached a mean breakpoint of 57.4 ± 4.6 lever presses for a single sucrose reward.
source: Across all cohorts, the animals in the top 25% of interquartile distribution (highS rats) reached a mean breakpoint of 270.4 ± 11.3 lever presses, whereas the animals in the bottom 25% of interquartile distribution (lowS rats) reached a mean breakpoint of 57.4 ± 4.6 lever presses for a single sucrose reward (Figure 1A; t(42)=26.35 p<0.0001, unpaired t-test).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data presented in Figure 1A with statistical analysis.

claim: HighS rats pressed the active lever an average of 1462 ± 59.2 times, while lowS rats pressed the active lever an average of 296.6 ± 21.2 times per single operant session.
source: HighS rats pressed the active lever an average of 1462 ± 59.2 times, while lowS rats pressed the active lever an average of 296.6 ± 21.2 times per single operant session (Figure 1B; t(42)=26.49 p<0.0001, unpaired t-test).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data presented in Figure 1B with statistical analysis.

claim: HighS rats earned an average of nine extra sucrose pellets in a single session relative to lowS rats.
source: This difference in operant responding corresponded to an average of nine extra sucrose pellets earned in a single session by highS, relative to lowS, rats (Figure 1C; highS: 19.25 ± 0.16 pellets; lowS: 10.9 ± 0.46 pellets, t(42)=16.36 p<0.0001, unpaired t-test).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data presented in Figure 1C with statistical analysis.

claim: The rats that would go on to form lowS and highS group acquired the self-administration task with a similar time course as the FR training progressed from 1 to 3 to 10 lever presses per reward.
source: The rats that would go on to form lowS and highS group acquired the self-administration task with a similar time course as the FR training progressed from 1 to 3 to 10 lever presses per reward (Figure 1F; [Main group effect: F(1,42)=2.13, p=0.1] two-way ANOVA).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data presented in Figure 1F with statistical analysis.

claim: The animals did not differ in the number of active lever presses over the final 3 days of FR10 training.
source: Similarly, the animals did not differ in the number of active lever presses (Figure 1G; t(42)=0.62, p=0.5442, unpaired t-test)
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data presented in Figure 1G with statistical analysis.

claim: There was no correlation between active lever presses on FR10 and breakpoints achieved on the PR schedule.
source: There was also no correlation between active lever presses on FR10 and breakpoints achieved on the PR schedule (Figure 1, Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Inactive lever presses were not different between lowS and highS rats on either the FR or the PR schedules of reinforcement.
source: Inactive lever presses were not different between lowS and highS rats on either the FR (lowS: 1.1 ± 0.52; highS: 0.75 ± 0.37; t(42)=0.54 p=0.59, unpaired Student's t-test) or the PR (lowS: 2.9 ± 0.6; highS: 3.9 ± 0.7; t(42)=1.07 p=0.29, unpaired Student's t-test) schedules of reinforcement
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data with statistical analysis.

claim: Corticosterone levels did not differ between rats.
source: Corticosterone levels did not differ between rats (Figure 2A)
evidence: This claim is supported by corticosterone measurement data presented in Figure 2A.

claim: There was no correlation between individual corticosterone levels and PR breakpoints.
source: and there was no correlation between individual corticosterone levels and PR breakpoints (Figure 2B; Pearson's r2 = 0.0005, p=0.93).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis presented in Figure 2B.

claim: The transcriptome profile diverged between, but not within, groups of rats characterized by their behavioral performance on the PR task.
source: However, we found that the transcriptome profile diverged between, but not within, groups of rats characterized by their behavioral performance on the PR task.

claim: The transcriptome of animals with intermediate performance on the PR schedule (midS) aligned closer to highS, rather than lowS, rats.

claim: Between the lowS and highS groups, a total of 231 transcripts were differentially regulated.
source: Between the lowS and highS groups, a total of 231 transcripts were differentially regulated (Figure 3, Figure 3—source data 1; log2fold values ≥ 0.5 or≤−0.5).

claim: Dopamine and K+ channel-related transcripts accounted for 3 of the top five gene pathways with significant differences in expression between lowS and highS groups.
source: This analysis indicated that dopamine and K+ channel-related transcripts accounted for 3 of the top five gene pathways with significant differences in expression between lowS and highS groups.
evidence: This claim is supported by pathway analysis of RNA sequencing data presented in Figure 3C.

claim: Four genes related to dopamine signaling (Pdyn, Drd1, Penk and Drd2) were expressed at significantly lower levels in the lowS group.

claim: Six genes related to K+ channel signaling (Hcn4, Kcna4, Kcnab1, Kcnc4, and Kcnv1) were bi-directionally regulated in the lowS relative to highS group.

claim: SPNs of lowS rats fired significantly more action potentials across a range of depolarizing current injections than SPNs of highS rats.

claim: Action potential waveform analysis showed decreased spike afterhyperpolarization in cells from lowS animals.

claim: Peak IA amplitude was not significantly different between lowS and highS groups across a range of holding potentials.

claim: The decay time of inactivation was 27% faster in lowS relative to highS animals.

claim: There was no difference in BK current amplitude (IBK) between lowS and highS groups.

claim: The overall effect of acute application of UK-78,282 (100 nM) was to suppress action potential output in lowS, but not highS, SPNs.
source: The overall effect of acute application of UK-78,282 (100 nM) was to suppress action potential output in lowS, but not highS, SPNs (Figure 5A).

claim: Application of UK-78,282 significantly reduced amplitude of the IA in lowS, highS, and midS rats.

claim: In neurons from highS animals, IA inactivation was insensitive to UK-78,282 with the time constant of 9.07 ± 1.3 ms at baseline and 8.9 ± 1.3 ms after UK-78,282 application.

claim: A higher dose of UK-78,282 (100 nM) significantly increased breakpoints in the lowS, but not the highS or midS groups.

claim: Active lever responding and pellets earned were increased specifically in the lowS rats following UK-78,282 (100 nM) microinjection.

source: The voltage-dependence of activation kinetics of Kv1 family members has been shown to shift in the depolarizing direction by assembly with Kv1.2 subunit (Baronas et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Baronas et al., 2015.

claim: Kv1.2 has been shown to enhance activation of Kv1.4/1.2 heterotetramers following depolarizing pre-pulses, a phenomenon termed use-dependent activation (Baronas et al., 2015).
source: Moreover, Kv1.2 has been shown to enhance activation of Kv1.4/1.2 heterotetramers following depolarizing pre-pulses, a phenomenon termed use-dependent activation (Baronas et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Baronas et al., 2015.

claim: Behavioral variability in motivation was specific to the high effort conditions imposed by the PR task.
source: This indicates that behavioral variability was specific to the high effort conditions imposed by the PR task.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of differences in FR performance but significant differences in PR performance between groups.

claim: Individual variability in motivation for sucrose is dissociable from performance on low-effort, fixed ratio tasks.
source: Altogether, these data indicate that individual variability in motivation for sucrose is dissociable from performance on low-effort, fixed ratio tasks.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the behavioral data showing no differences in FR performance but significant differences in PR performance.

claim: Variability in motivation is not due to differences in acquisition of stimulus-reward associations, locomotor ability, or baseline differences in HPA axis function.
source: Furthermore, variability in motivation that we report is not due to differences in acquisition of stimulus-reward associations, locomotor ability, or baseline differences in HPA axis function.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from behavioral and corticosterone data showing no differences in these measures between groups.

claim: Behavioral differences in motivation for reward are linked to genomic variability.
source: Overall, RNA sequencing data indicated that behavioral differences in motivation for reward are linked to genomic variability.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the RNA sequencing data showing differential gene expression between groups.

claim: Low effort-based motivation occurred on a background of increased membrane excitability.
source: Therefore, we speculated that low effort-based motivation occurred on a background of increased membrane excitability.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on RNA sequencing data and prior knowledge about NAc function.

claim: Increased spiking in lowS animals is consistent with faster A-type current inactivation and decreased spike afterhyperpolarization.
source: This increased spiking is consistent with faster A-type current inactivation and decreased spike afterhyperpolarization, but is not related to availability of IA and BK channels or overall ion permeability through voltage-gated K+ channels.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the electrophysiological data showing faster IA decay and decreased AHP in lowS animals.

claim: Differences in Kv1.4 gating, rather than number of available channels alters firing of NAc shell SPNs in a manner that may discriminate between behavioral extremes on a progressive ratio task.
source: We conclude that differences in Kv1.4 gating, rather than number of available channels alters firing of NAc shell SPNs in a manner that may discriminate between behavioral extremes on a progressive ratio task.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the electrophysiological data showing differential effects of UK-78,282 on IA kinetics but not amplitude.

claim: Decreased D2 receptor stimulation would lead to decreased CaMKII activity and faster A-type current inactivation.
source: If this mechanism were to be involved, then decreased D2 receptor stimulation would lead to decreased CaMKII activity and faster A-type current inactivation.
evidence: This is a speculative mechanism proposed to explain the observed differences in IA kinetics.

claim: Lower expression of Kvβ1 is expected to decrease availability of Kv1.x hetero-tetramers and contribute to faster Kv1.4 channel inactivation.
source: Lower expression of Kvβ1 is expected to decrease availability of Kv1.x hetero-tetramers and contribute to faster Kv1.4 channel inactivation reported here.
evidence: This is a speculative mechanism proposed to explain the observed differences in IA kinetics based on RNA sequencing data.

claim: Unique sensitivity of lowS NAc neurons to UK-78,282 is likely conferred by differential interaction of Kv1.4 channels with binding partners or phosphorylation mechanisms rather than functional availability of Kv1.4 channels on the cell surface.
source: We can conclude, however, that unique sensitivity of lowS NAc neurons to UK-78,282 is likely conferred by differential interaction of Kv1.4 channels with binding partners or phosphorylation mechanisms rather than functional availability of Kv1.4 channels on the cell surface.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the electrophysiological data showing differential effects of UK-78,282 on IA kinetics but similar effects on amplitude.

claim: Use-dependent activation may play a role in suppressing action potentials during spike trains and contribute to lower action potential spike frequency observed in highS animals.
source: Such use-dependence may play a role in suppressing action potentials during spike trains and contribute to lower action potential spike frequency observed in highS animals.
evidence: This is a speculative mechanism proposed to explain the observed differences in spike frequency.

claim: Slower inactivation of IA in highS animals will tend to suppress action potential output.
source: Slower inactivation of IA in highS animals, discussed above, will also tend to suppress action potential output.
evidence: This is an inference based on the known relationship between IA inactivation kinetics and neuronal firing.

claim: Any behavior encoded by NAc shell output will be biased by greater intrinsic likelihood of generating such output by SPNs in lowS, relative to highS, animals.
source: Our data do support the idea that any behavior encoded by NAc shell output will be biased by greater intrinsic likelihood of generating such output by SPNs in lowS, relative to highS, animals.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the electrophysiological data showing increased excitability in lowS animals.

claim: Lower motivation is linked to a divergent transcriptome profile, and increased SPN output in the NAc shell.
source: In summary, we describe a set of neuronal and genetic features associated with motivation to exert effort for natural reward. Lower motivation is linked to a divergent transcriptome profile, and increased SPN output in the NAc shell.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the RNA sequencing and electrophysiological data.

claim: Increased SPN output depends on faster inactivation kinetics of Kv1.4.
source: Increased SPN output depends on faster inactivation kinetics of Kv1.4
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the electrophysiological data showing faster IA decay in lowS animals and the effects of UK-78,282.

claim: Blockade of Kv1.4 activity selectively increases effort for natural reward in animals displaying low motivation.
source: and blockade of Kv1.4 activity selectively increases effort for natural reward in animals displaying low motivation.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the behavioral data showing selective effects of UK-78,282 microinjection in lowS animals.

claim: Modulators of Kv1.4 gating are potential targets in a broad spectrum of psychiatric disorders associated with deficits in motivation.
source: These results point to modulators of Kv1.4 gating as potential targets in a broad spectrum of psychiatric disorders associated with deficits in motivation.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion about potential therapeutic applications based on the study findings.

claim: Seven cohorts totaling 111 rats were used to profile behavioral motivation for sucrose reward using a PR schedule of reinforcement.
source: We began by establishing a behavioral profile of motivation for sucrose reward using a PR schedule of reinforcement in seven cohorts totaling 111 rats (Figure 1, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design and sample size.

claim: Animals were assigned to categories following 3 days of stable responding (<10% variability in active lever presses) on the PR schedule.
source: To ensure that responding on PR was a stable behavior, animals were assigned to categories following 3 days of stable responding (<10% variability in active lever presses) on the PR schedule (Figure 1D,E).
evidence: This describes the criteria used for categorizing animals into groups.

claim: Seeking of natural rewards and behavioral performance on progressive ratio schedules of reinforcement critically relies on activity of the NAc shell (Basso and Kelley, 1999; Reynolds and Berridge, 2001; Kelley and Swanson, 1997; Wirtshafter and Stratford, 2010).
source: Seeking of natural rewards and behavioral performance on progressive ratio schedules of reinforcement critically relies on activity of the NAc shell (Basso and Kelley, 1999; Reynolds and Berridge, 2001; Kelley and Swanson, 1997; Wirtshafter and Stratford, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Fast-inactivating A-type currents are mediated by K+ channel proteins encoded by Kcna4, Kcnc4, or Kcnd1-3 genes (Coetzee et al., 1999).
source: Fast-inactivating A-type currents are mediated by K+ channel proteins encoded by Kcna4, Kcnc4, or Kcnd1-3 genes (Coetzee et al., 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Coetzee et al., 1999.

claim: Action potential frequency is strongly sensitive to IA inactivation kinetics (Zemel et al., 2018).
source: However, action potential output is strongly sensitive to IA inactivation kinetics (Zemel et al., 2018)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Zemel et al., 2018.

claim: Faster inactivation is expected to increase action potential frequency similarly to the effect of reduction in the number of underlying channels.
source: with faster inactivation expected to increase action potential frequency similarly to the effect of reduction in the number of underlying channels (see Discussion).
evidence: This is an inference based on established knowledge about the relationship between channel kinetics and neuronal firing.

claim: BK channels have been shown to interact with IA to influence both afterhyperpolarization and neuronal firing (Kimm et al., 2015; Storm, 1987; Zhang and McBain, 1995).
source: We then looked at currents mediated by the large-conductance Ca2+-activated potassium (BK) channels since they have been shown to interact with IA to influence both afterhyperpolarization and neuronal firing (Kimm et al., 2015; Storm, 1987; Zhang and McBain, 1995).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Recordings from midS animals aligned with findings in highS subjects: spike frequency was lower than the lowS group, but did not differ from highS animals.
source: Finally, recordings from midS animals aligned with findings in highS subjects: spike frequency was lower than the lowS group, but did not differ from highS animals
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data presented in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: IA amplitude, IBK, and total K+ currents did not differ between lowS, midS and highS groups.
source: while IA amplitude, IBK, and total K+ currents did not differ between lowS, midS and highS groups (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data presented in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: IA decay time in the midS group was intermediate to that of lowS and highS animals and not significantly different from either group.
source: Notably, IA decay time in the midS group was intermediate to that of lowS and highS animals and not significantly different from either group (Figure 4—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data presented in Figure 4—figure supplement 2C.

claim: A low motivation phenotype is linked to increased spiking of NAc principal neurons.
source: Overall, our results suggest that a low motivation phenotype is linked to increased spiking of NAc principal neurons.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the electrophysiological data.

claim: UK-78,282 had a similar effect on afterhyperpolarization area in both lowS and highS animals.
source: UK-78,282 had a similar effect on afterhyperpolarization area in both lowS and highS animals (Figure 5C)
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data presented in Figure 5C.

claim: Kv1.4 activity does not account for differences in afterhyperpolarization between lowS and highS group at baseline.
source: suggesting that Kv1.4 activity does not account for differences in afterhyperpolarization between lowS and highS group at baseline (cf. Figure 4B).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that UK-78,282 had similar effects on AHP in both groups.

claim: UK-78,282 application did not result in significant differences between lowS and highS groups across a battery of excitability measures.
source: Additionally, UK-78,282 application did not result in significant differences between lowS and highS groups across a battery of excitability measures (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data presented in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Spike frequency in midS animals was not affected by UK-78,282.
source: Similar to highS animals, spike frequency in midS animals was not affected by UK-78,282 (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data presented in Figure 5—figure supplement 2A.

claim: AHP in the midS group and IBK in either lowS, midS, or highS groups was unaffected by UK-78,282.
source: AHP in the midS group and IBK in either lowS, midS, or highS groups was also unaffected (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B–E).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data presented in Figure 5—figure supplement 2B–E.

claim: In lowS animals, UK-78,282 application reduced IA current amplitude across all voltages, including the voltage range subthreshold to action potential firing.
source: In the lowS animals, our results indicate equal availability of Kv1.4 across potentials, including in the zone subthreshold to action potential firing.
evidence: This is inferred from the voltage-dependence data showing UK-78,282 effects across all voltages in lowS animals.

claim: In highS animals, IA was suppressed by UK-78,282 only at higher depolarizing voltages.
source: In the highS animals, Kv1.4 availability is greater at suprathreshold potentials.
evidence: This is inferred from the voltage-dependence data showing UK-78,282 effects primarily at higher voltages in highS animals.

claim: There was no effect of UK-78,282 on IA decay time in midS animals.
source: There was no effect of UK-78,282 on IA decay time in midS animals (Figure 5—figure supplement 2G,t(6)=0.35, p=0.74, paired t-test).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data presented in Figure 5—figure supplement 2G with statistical analysis.

claim: The low dose of UK-78,282 (1 nM) had no significant effect on sucrose self-administration in any group.
source: The low dose of UK-78,282 (1 nM) had no significant effect on sucrose self-administration in any group.
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data from microinjection experiments presented in Figure 6.

claim: There was no difference in inactive lever presses between UK-78,282 concentrations in the lowS or midS groups.
source: There was no difference in inactive lever presses between UK-78,282 concentrations in the lowS or midS groups (lowS: F(2,21)=0.75, p=0.5; midS: F(2,25)=0.14, p=0.86, one-way ANOVAs)
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data from microinjection experiments with statistical analysis.

claim: Inactive lever pressing was significantly reduced by UK-78,282 (100 nM) in highS rats.
source: although inactive lever pressing was significantly reduced by UK-78,282 (100 nM) in highS rats (F(2,21)=6.1, p=0.008, one-way ANOVA; Figure 6Aiv, Biv, Civ).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data from microinjection experiments presented in Figure 6 with statistical analysis.

claim: An antagonist of Kv1.4 channels elevates willingness to exert effort for reward selectively in rats displaying lower motivation.
source: Overall, these data show that an antagonist of Kv1.4 channels elevates willingness to exert effort for reward selectively in rats displaying lower motivation.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the behavioral microinjection data.

claim: At 100 nM concentration, UK-78,282 is expected to be highly specific for Kv1.4.
source: At this concentration, UK-78,282 is expected to be highly specific for Kv1.4.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about UK-78,282 selectivity cited earlier in the manuscript.

claim: Reduced Kcna4 transcript in lowS animals did not reduce availability of Kv1.4 at the cell surface relative to highS group.
source: This was an unexpected result suggesting that reduced Kcna4 transcript in lowS animals did not reduce availability of Kv1.4 at the cell surface relative to highS group.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that UK-78,282 reduced IA amplitude equally in both groups despite differential Kcna4 expression.

claim: No significant differences were detected in expression of any of the four major CaMKII isoform genes (Camk2a, Camk2b, Camk2d, and Camk2g) in the RNA sequencing data.
source: We detected no significant differences in expression of any of the four major CaMKII isoform genes (Camk2a, Camk2b, Camk2d, and Camk2g) in the RNA sequencing data.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA sequencing data.

claim: Sequencing data show significant downregulation of Drd2 and upregulation of Camk2n2 (but not Camk2n1) transcripts in the lowS, relative to the highS, NAc tissue.
source: Consistent with this, our sequencing data show significant downregulation of Drd2 and upregulation of Camk2n2 (but not Camk2n1), transcripts in the lowS, relative to the highS, NAc tissue (Figure 3A, Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA sequencing data presented in Figure 3.

claim: Neither Kcna1 nor Kcna2 were differentially expressed in the lowS vs highS sequencing data.
source: Neither Kcna1 nor Kcna2 were differentially expressed in the lowS vs highS sequencing data.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA sequencing data.

claim: Expression of the regulatory subunit Kvβ1 (Kcnab1 gene) was markedly lower in the NAc of lowS animals.
source: However, expression of the regulatory subunit Kvβ1 (Kcnab1 gene) that promotes cell surface expression of Kv1.x heterotetrameric complexes (Manganas and Trimmer, 2000) was markedly lower in the NAc of lowS animals.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA sequencing data.

claim: RNA sequencing data from midS animals indicated significantly lower levels of Kcna1 and Kcnab2 transcripts.
source: It is intriguing that with regard to possible regulators of Kv1.4 function discussed above, RNA sequencing data from midS animals indicated significantly lower levels of Kcna1 and Kcnab2 transcripts
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA sequencing data.

claim: RNA sequencing data from midS animals showed decreased Camk2n1 (no change in Camk2n2) levels.
source: but decreased Camk2n1 (no change in Camk2n2) levels expected to lead to slower inactivation (Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA sequencing data.

claim: LowS and highS groups are similar across a broad spectrum of action potential and intrinsic excitability measures both in the absence and in the presence of UK-78,282.
source: Indeed, we observe that lowS and highS groups are similar across a broad spectrum of action potential and intrinsic excitability measures both in the absence and in the presence of UK-78,282 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data presented in supplementary figures.

claim: There is general support from behavioral pharmacology studies that inhibition of NAc shell promotes seeking of natural reward.
source: There is general support from behavioral pharmacology studies that inhibition of NAc shell promotes seeking of natural reward (Basso and Kelley, 1999; Reynolds and Berridge, 2001; Kelley and Swanson, 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Random selection of SPNs from the pool of visually identified neurons and similar input resistance and rheobase values between groups argue against biased sampling of D1 or D2 neurons.
source: However, several considerations argue against biased sampling, including random selection of SPNs from the pool of visually identified neurons and similar input resistance and rheobase values, hallmarks of D1 or D2 identity (Gertler et al., 2008; Janssen et al., 2009), between groups.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental methods and electrophysiological data.

claim: RNA sequencing results indicated reduced expression of both D1 dopamine receptor and D2 dopamine receptor encoding genes in lowS relative to highS animals.
source: RNA sequencing results indicated reduced expression of both D1 dopamine receptor and D2 dopamine receptor encoding genes in lowS relative to highS animals, rather than a selective reduction of one receptor population.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA sequencing data.

claim: Effort-based motivation for natural reward is unlikely to depend on a uniformly sustained increase or decrease in firing across all NAc shell SPNs.
source: Effort-based motivation for natural reward is unlikely to depend on a uniformly sustained increase or decrease in firing across all NAc shell SPNs.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from consideration of prior in vivo electrophysiology studies.

claim: Behavioral output during progressive ratio for cocaine involved some neurons that are excited and others that are inhibited throughout the different phases of a behavioral task (Nicola and Deadwyler, 2000).
source: However, behavioral output during progressive ratio for cocaine involved some neurons that are excited and others that are inhibited throughout the different phases of a behavioral task (Nicola and Deadwyler, 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Nicola and Deadwyler, 2000.

claim: Responses combining both excitation and inhibition have been observed in the NAc across many reward-seeking behaviors examined with in vivo electrophysiology.
source: Indeed, responses combining both excitation and inhibition have been observed in the NAc across many reward-seeking behaviors examined with in vivo electrophysiology.
evidence: This statement draws from established knowledge in the field of NAc electrophysiology.

claim: Dynamic responses in NAc may be guided by interactions with a distinct pattern of inputs to or outputs from the NAc.
source: It is possible that such dynamic responses are guided by interactions with a distinct pattern of inputs to or outputs from the NAc and our experiments do not address this contingency.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about possible mechanisms not tested in the study.
